intro.x: A distribution can be encoded in a function whose algebra matches the algebra of sums of independent variables. Three such encodings are used throughout probability: the moment generating function, the probability generating function (for integer-valued variables), and the characteristic function (which always exists). They turn convolutions into products, make moments computable by differentiation, and are the main tool in the proof of the central limit theorem.

blocks.x: For $k\ge1$ the $k$th moment of $X$ is $\Exp[X^k]$ and the $k$th central moment is $\Exp[(X-\mu)^k]$, provided $\Exp\abs X^k<\infty$. The skewness is $\Exp[(X-\mu)^3]/\sigma^3$ and the kurtosis is $\Exp[(X-\mu)^4]/\sigma^4$.
If $\Exp\abs X^s<\infty$ and $0<r<s$, then $\Exp\abs X^r<\infty$.
For every real $x$, $\abs x^r\le1+\abs x^s$ (if $\abs x\le1$ then $\abs x^r\le1$; otherwise $\abs x^r\le\abs x^s$). Take expectations.
The converse is false: the distribution with density $\propto x^{-4}$ on $x>1$ has a finite mean and variance but infinite third moment.
The moment generating function of $X$ is $M_X(t)=\Exp[e^{tX}]$ for those real $t$ for which the expectation is finite. We assume it is finite on an open interval around $t=0$ whenever we use it.
If $M_X(t)<\infty$ for $\abs t<\delta$ for some $\delta>0$, then all moments exist and $M_X$ is infinitely differentiable on $(-\delta,\delta)$, with

\Exp[X^k]=M_X^{(k)}(0),\qquad
M_X(t)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{\Exp[X^k]}{k!}t^k\quad(\abs t<\delta).

Fix $0<t<\delta$. Finiteness of $\Exp[e^{tX}]$ and $\Exp[e^{-tX}]$ implies $\Exp[e^{t\abs X}]\le\Exp[e^{tX}]+\Exp[e^{-tX}]<\infty$, because $e^{t\abs x}\le e^{tx}+e^{-tx}$. Since $e^{t\abs x}\ge(t\abs x)^k/k!$ for every $k$, we get $\Exp\abs X^k\le k!\,\Exp[e^{t\abs X}]/t^k<\infty$. Expanding $e^{tX}=\sum_k(tX)^k/k!$ and interchanging expectation with the sum (justified by dominated convergence with the bound $\sum_k\abs{tX}^k/k!=e^{\abs{tX}}$, which has finite expectation; see Chapter 15) gives the power series, whose coefficients are $M_X^{(k)}(0)/k!$.
$M_{aX+b}(t)=e^{bt}M_X(at)$.
If $X,Y$ are independent, $M_{X+Y}(t)=M_X(t)M_Y(t)$.
(Uniqueness, cited) If $M_X=M_Y<\infty$ on an interval around $0$, then $X$ and $Y$ have the same distribution.

(i) $\Exp[e^{t(aX+b)}]=e^{bt}\Exp[e^{(at)X}]$. (ii) $e^{tX}$ and $e^{tY}$ are independent (functions of independent variables), so by Theorem 6.6 the expectation of the product is the product of expectations. (iii) is a deep theorem; it follows from the uniqueness of the Laplace transform (or from Fourier inversion for the characteristic function in Section 9.4), and we use it without proof.
Computations

Derivations. Poisson: $\sum_ke^{tk}e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!=e^{-\lambda}\exp(\lambda e^t)$. Exponential: $\int_0^\infty e^{tx}\lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx=\lambda/(\lambda-t)$ for $t<\lambda$. Gamma: the substitution $u=(\lambda-t)x$ in the gamma integral. For the standard normal, complete the square, $tz-z^2/2=-(z-t)^2/2+t^2/2$:
M_Z(t)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int e^{tz-z^2/2}dz=e^{t^2/2}\cdot\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int e^{-(z-t)^2/2}dz=e^{t^2/2},
and then $M_{\mu+\sigma Z}(t)=e^{\mu t}M_Z(\sigma t)$ by (i).

MGFs give instant proofs of the closure theorems. If $X\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$, $Y\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)$ are independent then $M_{X+Y}=\exp((\lambda+\mu)(e^t-1))$, so $X+Y\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda+\mu)$ by uniqueness. Likewise, normals add by adding exponents; and a sum of $n$ independent Exp$(\lambda)$ has MGF $(\lambda/(\lambda-t))^n$, the Gamma$(n,\lambda)$ MGF.

Since $M_Z(t)=e^{t^2/2}=\sum_m\frac{t^{2m}}{2^mm!}$, matching with $\sum_k\Exp[Z^k]t^k/k!$ gives $\Exp[Z^{2m}]=\frac{(2m)!}{2^mm!}=(2m-1)!!$ and all odd moments zero. So $\Exp[Z^4]=3$ (kurtosis $3$, the benchmark for “normal tails”).

Heavy-tailed distributions have no MGF: the log-normal and Cauchy distributions have $\Exp[e^{tX}]=\infty$ for every $t>0$. Moreover, having all moments finite is not enough for the moments to determine the distribution: the log-normal distribution has finite moments of every order but shares them with other distributions. Existence of the MGF in a neighbourhood of $0$ is a sufficient condition for determinacy.
Cumulants

The cumulant generating function is $K_X(t)=\ln M_X(t)$, and its derivatives at zero are the cumulants $\kappa_1,\kappa_2,\dots$ Because $M_{X+Y}=M_XM_Y$ for independent variables, $K_{X+Y}=K_X+K_Y$, so cumulants are additive. The first two are the mean and variance, $\kappa_3$ is the third central moment. For the normal, $K(t)=\mu t+\sigma^2t^2/2$, so all cumulants beyond the second vanish; for the Poisson, $K(t)=\lambda(e^t-1)$, so every cumulant equals $\lambda$.
For a random variable $N$ taking values in $\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ with $p_k=\Prob(N=k)$, the probability generating function (PGF) is
G_N(s)=\Exp[s^N]=\sum_{k=0}^\infty p_ks^k,\qquad\abs s\le1.
The series converges absolutely for $\abs s\le1$ since $\sum p_k=1$.
$G_N(1)=1$ and $G_N$ determines the PMF: $p_k=G_N^{(k)}(0)/k!$.
$\Exp[N]=G_N'(1^-)$ and $\Exp[N(N-1)]=G_N''(1^-)$ (derivatives from the left; both sides may be $+\infty$), so $\Var(N)=G''(1)+G'(1)-G'(1)^2$.
If $N,M$ are independent, $G_{N+M}=G_NG_M$.

(i) A power series is determined by its coefficients, and the Taylor coefficients are $G^{(k)}(0)/k!$. (ii) Differentiating the power series term by term for $\abs s<1$ gives $G'(s)=\sum kp_ks^{k-1}$ and $G''(s)=\sum k(k-1)p_ks^{k-2}$; let $s\uparrow1$ using monotone convergence (all terms are non-negative). (iii) $s^{N+M}=s^Ns^M$ with independent factors.

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Random sums: Wald’s identity and compound variance

blocks.x: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. non-negative integer-valued with PGF $G_X$, and let $N$ be independent of the $X_i$, also non-negative integer-valued with PGF $G_N$. Then $S=\sum_{i=1}^NX_i$ has PGF $G_S(s)=G_N\bigl(G_X(s)\bigr)$. If the means and variances are finite,
\Exp[S]=\Exp[N]\Exp[X],\qquad\Var(S)=\Exp[N]\Var(X)+\Var(N)\,(\Exp[X])^2.
Condition on $N$ (law of total probability for expectations over the partition $\{N=n\}$):
G_S(s)=\sum_n\Prob(N=n)\,\Exp\bigl[s^{X_1+\dots+X_n}\bigr]=\sum_n\Prob(N=n)G_X(s)^n=G_N(G_X(s)).

Differentiating, $G_S'(s)=G_N'(G_X(s))G_X'(s)$, so $G_S'(1)=G_N'(1)G_X'(1)$ (as $G_X(1)=1$), which is the mean formula. Differentiating again, $G_S''(1)=G_N''(1)G_X'(1)^2+G_N'(1)G_X''(1)$, and substituting into $\Var(S)=G_S''(1)+G_S'(1)-G_S'(1)^2$ and simplifying with $G''(1)=\Exp[X(X-1)]$ gives the variance formula.

Each of $N\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$ customers independently buys with probability $p$. The number of buyers is $S=\sum_{i\le N}X_i$ with $X_i\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$, $G_X(s)=q+ps$. Then $G_S(s)=\exp\bigl(\lambda(q+ps-1)\bigr)=\exp\bigl(\lambda p(s-1)\bigr)$, which is the Poisson$(\lambda p)$ PGF. So thinning a Poisson count gives a Poisson count.
Branching processes and extinction

Start with one individual. Each individual independently has $\xi$ children, with PMF $p_k$ and PGF $G$. Let $Z_n$ be the size of generation $n$ and $\pi=\Prob(\text{eventual extinction})$. By conditioning on the first generation: if the root has $k$ children, each of the $k$ independent subtrees dies out with probability $\pi$, so
\pi=\sum_kp_k\pi^k=G(\pi).
Assume $p_1<1$. The extinction probability is the smallest root of $s=G(s)$ in $[0,1]$. If $\Exp[\xi]=G'(1)\le1$ then $\pi=1$; if $\Exp[\xi]>1$ then $\pi<1$.

Let $\pi_n=\Prob(Z_n=0)$. By the same conditioning, $\pi_{n+1}=G(\pi_n)$ with $\pi_0=0$. The events $\{Z_n=0\}$ increase to the extinction event, so $\pi_n\uparrow\pi$ by continuity (Theorem 2.10), and since $G$ is continuous, $\pi=G(\pi)$. If $s^*$ is any root of $s=G(s)$ in $[0,1]$, then $\pi_0=0\le s^*$ and, $G$ being non-decreasing, $\pi_{n+1}=G(\pi_n)\le G(s^*)=s^*$ by induction; hence $\pi\le s^*$, so $\pi$ is the smallest root. $G$ is convex on $[0,1]$ (non-negative coefficients), $G(1)=1$. If $G'(1)\le1$ the graph of $G$ lies above the diagonal on $[0,1)$ (convexity plus slope at most $1$ at $s=1$, using $p_1<1$ for strictness), so the only root is $1$. If $G'(1)>1$, then $G(s)<s$ for $s$ slightly below $1$, while $G(0)\ge0$, so by continuity there is a root in $[0,1)$.

For instance with offspring law $p_0=\tfrac14,p_1=\tfrac14,p_2=\tfrac12$: the mean is $\tfrac54>1$ and $s=\tfrac14+\tfrac14s+\tfrac12s^2$ gives $2s^2-3s+1=0$, i.e. $s=\tfrac12$ or $s=1$. So $\pi=\tfrac12$.
The characteristic function of $X$ is $\varphi_X(t)=\Exp[e^{itX}]=\Exp[\cos tX]+i\,\Exp[\sin tX]$, for $t\in\R$.
Unlike the MGF it always exists, because $\abs{e^{itX}}=1$.
$\varphi_X(0)=1$, $\abs{\varphi_X(t)}\le1$, and $\varphi_X(-t)=\overline{\varphi_X(t)}$.
$\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$.
If $X,Y$ are independent, $\varphi_{X+Y}=\varphi_X\varphi_Y$.

(Moments, cited) If $\Exp\abs X^k<\infty$ then $\varphi_X$ is $k$ times continuously differentiable and $\varphi_X^{(k)}(0)=i^k\Exp[X^k]$. In particular, $\varphi_X(t)=1+it\Exp[X]-\tfrac12t^2\Exp[X^2]+o(t^2)$ when $\Exp[X^2]<\infty$.
(Uniqueness, cited) $\varphi_X=\varphi_Y$ implies $X\overset d=Y$.
(L'evy continuity theorem, cited; proved in Chapter 15) $X_n\xrightarrow{d}X$ iff $\varphi_{X_n}(t)\to\varphi_X(t)$ for every $t$ (where the limit function is continuous at $0$).

(i) $\abs{\Exp[e^{itX}]}\le\Exp\abs{e^{itX}}=1$; conjugation: $\overline{e^{itX}}=e^{-itX}$. (ii) $e^{it(aX+b)}=e^{itb}e^{i(at)X}$. (iii) As for MGFs, $e^{itX}$ and $e^{itY}$ are independent and bounded.
$\varphi_Z(t)=e^{-t^2/2}$. Derivation by differential equation. Differentiating under the integral (justified since $\abs{xe^{itx}\varphi(x)}$ is integrable),

\varphi_Z'(t)=\int ix e^{itx}\varphi(x)\,dx=-i\int e^{itx}\varphi'(x)\,dx
=-i\Bigl([e^{itx}\varphi(x)]_{-\infty}^\infty-it\int e^{itx}\varphi(x)\,dx\Bigr)=-t\varphi_Z(t),
using $x\varphi=-\varphi'$ and integration by parts. With $\varphi_Z(0)=1$ the unique solution is $e^{-t^2/2}$. Hence $\varphi_{N(\mu,\sigma^2)}(t)=e^{i\mu t-\sigma^2t^2/2}$.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Cauchy: the law of large numbers fails

blocks.x: The standard Cauchy has $\varphi(t)=e^{-\abs t}$. Derivation. Start from the two-sided exponential density $\tfrac12e^{-\abs x}$, whose characteristic function is $\tfrac12\int e^{-\abs x}e^{itx}dx=\tfrac12\bigl(\tfrac1{1-it}+\tfrac1{1+it}\bigr)=\tfrac1{1+t^2}$. The Fourier inversion theorem (cited here, proved in Chapter 15) says that when $\varphi$ is integrable the density is $f(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\int\varphi(t)e^{-itx}dt$. Applying this with $\varphi(t)=\frac1{1+t^2}$ and $f(x)=\tfrac12e^{-\abs x}$ gives $\tfrac12e^{-\abs x}=\frac1{2\pi}\int\frac{e^{-itx}}{1+t^2}dt$, i.e. $\int\frac{e^{itx}}{\pi(1+t^2)}\,dt=e^{-\abs x}$. Read with the roles of $t$ and $x$ swapped, this says exactly that the Cauchy density $\frac1{\pi(1+x^2)}$ has characteristic function $e^{-\abs t}$. If $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are i.i.d. standard Cauchy, the sample mean has
\varphi_{\bar X_n}(t)=\Bigl(\varphi\bigl(\tfrac tn\bigr)\Bigr)^n=\bigl(e^{-\abs t/n}\bigr)^n=e^{-\abs t},

so $\bar X_n$ is again standard Cauchy for every $n$. Averaging does nothing: the distribution of $\bar X_n$ never concentrates. The law of large numbers (next chapters) requires a finite mean. This also gives a short proof of the stability claim in Exercise 5 of Chapter 8.

Use the PGF for non-negative integer variables, especially for random sums and branching processes; the MGF for tail bounds (Chernoff, Chapter 10) and quick moment computations when it exists; the characteristic function when you need existence for every distribution (limit theorems). All three satisfy “transform of a sum of independents equals product of transforms”.
Compute the MGF of the geometric distribution and use it to rederive $\Exp[X]=1/p$ and $\Var(X)=q/p^2$.
Show that if $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ then $G_X(s)=(q+ps)^n$, and use Theorem 9.8 to recover the mean and variance.
Find the distribution of $N_1+N_2$ if $N_i$ are independent Geom$(p)$ using PGFs.
Let $X\sim N(0,1)$. Show that $\Exp[e^{tX^2}]=(1-2t)^{-1/2}$ for $t<\frac12$ and deduce that $X^2\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$.
A fair die is rolled; if the result is $N$, then $N$ fair coins are tossed. Find the mean and variance of the number of heads using Theorem 9.9.
Compute the extinction probability of a branching process with offspring distribution Poisson$(2)$ numerically (solve $s=e^{2(s-1)}$).
Prove: if $X$ has an MGF finite near $0$ and $\Exp[X]=0$, then $M_X(t)=1+\tfrac12\Var(X)t^2+O(t^3)$.
Show that $\varphi_X$ is real-valued if and only if $X$ and $-X$ have the same distribution.
(Challenge) Prove that the characteristic function is uniformly continuous on $\R$ (Hint: $\abs{\varphi(t+h)-\varphi(t)}\le\Exp\abs{e^{ihX}-1}$ and dominated convergence).
